high_priority_articles.title: India, UK to exchange tariff usage data under trade agreement - Livemint
high_priority_articles.summary: India, UK to exchange tariff usage data under trade agreement  Livemint
high_priority_articles.full_text:
New Delhi: India and the United Kingdom on Monday agreed to exchange annual data on businesses' utilisation of preferential tariffs under their Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), the commerce & industry ministry said in a statement. The two sides agreed to establish committees, working groups and government-to-government contact points to ensure the smooth implementation of the trade pact, it added.
The decision was taken at the 16th meeting of the India-UK Joint Economic and Trade Committee (JETCO) in New Delhi, co-chaired by commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal and UK secretary of state for business, innovation, science and trade Jonathan Reynolds, the ministry said in a joint statement.
Under the arrangement, the two countries will begin exchanging data one year after CETA came into force on 15 July 2026, including information on how frequently businesses claim lower tariffs available under the agreement. The exercise will also incorporate feedback from businesses on implementation challenges and areas requiring further support.
"We agreed that we will exchange data annually starting one year after the date of entry into force of the CETA on how businesses are using the agreement," the joint statement said.
The two sides said the mechanism would help identify priorities and enable more companies, particularly small and medium-sized businesses, to benefit from the agreement. The ministers welcomed the cooperation that had helped resolve issues during the initial implementation phase and asked officials to address any emerging challenges quickly.
The meeting marked the first JETCO since negotiations for CETA began in January 2022. Both countries reviewed progress since the agreement entered into force and discussed priorities for the coming year.
According to the joint statement, Indian exporters dispatched more than 50 consignments to the UK on the day the agreement entered into force, covering products such as smartphones, electrical and mechanical machinery, including turbojets, gold jewellery, ready-made garments, woollen yarn, tea and coffee.
The first shipment of Joha rice from Assam to the UK also took place, marking the first export of the distinctive regional variety to the British market.
The first certificates of origin under CETA were issued through India's eCoO 2.0 platform on a self-certification basis, facilitating exporters' access to preferential tariff treatment.
On the UK side, the first tariff-free Scottish salmon reached India within a fortnight of the agreement entering into force, with several thousand kilograms exported since then.
Scotch whisky has also entered the Indian market with reduced tariffs, while the first cars exported under the tariff-rate quota have cleared customs and been imported into India, the statement said.
Beyond merchandise trade, the two countries agreed to deepen cooperation in services, innovation, government procurement, science and technology, and gender-related areas, alongside greater business-to-business engagement and regional partnerships.
The ministers also welcomed the India-UK Science and Innovation Council meeting and the Innovation Roundtable, held on Monday, noting their role in connecting businesses, investors and researchers and accelerating the commercialisation of new technologies.
The JETCO meeting coincided with a visit by seven mayors and a combined authority leader from the North of England, alongside broader engagements involving government representatives, businesses, universities, innovators and regional leaders.
Both sides agreed to continue gathering feedback from businesses, industry associations, export promotion bodies and other stakeholders to identify and address implementation issues under CETA.
The ministers also supported continued visits by high-level delegations to sustain engagement between the two countries.
The 17th meeting of JETCO will be held in the United Kingdom in 2027, the statement said.

high_priority_articles.title: US tariffs accelerate global trade realignment: How India’s FTAs could boost GDP - Livemint
high_priority_articles.summary: US tariffs accelerate global trade realignment: How India’s FTAs could boost GDP  Livemint
high_priority_articles.full_text:
India’s expanding network of free trade agreements (FTAs) could add around $140 billion to its gross domestic product (GDP) by 2035 and increase exports by 6.2%, according to a report by Bloomberg Economics.
The report said the agreements could help India access new markets, lower import costs, attract foreign direct investment (FDI) and improve productivity as countries increasingly diversify supply chains and seek preferential access to overseas markets.
“Using a large-scale model of the global economy developed by the World Trade Organisation, we estimate these agreements could add about $140 billion to India’s GDP in 2035, opening new markets, cutting import costs, fostering foreign direct investment and lifting productivity,” said the Bloomberg report.
“We also consider two scenarios that could amplify the gains: realising further productivity benefits from a decade of reforms to strengthen manufacturing competitiveness, and enacting policies that help underemployed agricultural workers transition into manufacturing and services,” the report added.
The expansion of India’s trade network comes as rising US tariffs reshape global trade flows. Since President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, the United States has increased tariffs on several trading partners and product categories.
According to Bloomberg Economics, the average US tariff rate stood at 10.7% in August, compared with 2.3% in 2024. The increase reflected sector-specific duties, particularly on automobiles and metals, as well as country-specific levies.
The report said tariffs at these levels could reduce US imports of goods by around 15% compared with the previous regime. Further increases remain possible amid continuing tariff threats and investigations.
In response, economies are seeking to diversify their trade relationships and accelerate negotiations with new partners, creating opportunities for countries that can secure preferential market access.
India expands trade partnerships across major markets
India has accelerated its FTA programme after years of relative caution. During 2025-26, agreements with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), the United Kingdom and Oman entered into force, adding to trade agreements with Australia and the United Arab Emirates that took effect in 2022.
India also signed an FTA with New Zealand and concluded negotiations on a trade agreement with the European Union. New Delhi is pursuing additional partnerships, including with the Eurasian Economic Union, and has sought an agreement with the Gulf Cooperation Council.
Other major economies are following a similar approach. The European Union has signed new or updated agreements with Mercosur and Mexico and concluded negotiations with Indonesia, India and Australia. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations and China signed an upgraded free trade agreement in October 2025, while Canada has also pursued several trade agreements.
US-India trade negotiations remain important
Despite expanding its trade links elsewhere, India has continued efforts to deepen economic ties with the United States.
President Trump and Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced plans for a bilateral trade agreement in February 2025. However, negotiations have taken place against a backdrop of tariff tensions.
In the second half of 2025, India faced some of the highest additional US tariffs among its major trading partners after Washington imposed a 25% reciprocal tariff and an additional 25% duty on purchases of Russian oil.
Bloomberg Economics’ estimates suggest that India’s expanding trade agreements could support long-term growth by improving market access and strengthening its position in global supply chains. The extent of the benefits will also depend on domestic reforms, manufacturing competitiveness and the ability to shift workers into higher-productivity sectors.

high_priority_articles.title: Amata CEO Vikrom Kromadit built his industrial park empire in Thailand and Vietnam. Laos is next - Fortune
high_priority_articles.summary: Amata CEO Vikrom Kromadit built his industrial park empire in Thailand and Vietnam. Laos is next  Fortune
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Thai real estate developer Amata Corporation says Laos will become its “largest focus” in the years to come, CEO Vikrom Kromadit tells Fortune.
“Laos will become our largest focus because of the land bank that they have,” Kromadit tells Fortune. “They also have lots of green energy—that’s why they’re called the battery of Southeast Asia.”
Amata expanded into Laos in 2022, starting with Amata City Namor, which covers 31.5 square kilometers and sits beside a station on the China-Laos Railway. The company says its long-term Laos vision could reach 200 square kilometers.
Kromadit’s company built its fortunes in Thailand and Vietnam. Amata Corporation, founded in 1989, built industrial parks across Thailand’s Rayong and Chon Buri provinces. It was also an early backer of Vietnam, building its first facility there in 1994, early in the Southeast Asian country’s reform program. Laos, however, offers an opportunity for Amata to capture Chinese manufacturers expanding to new manufacturing hubs in Southeast Asia.
Laos, Southeast Asia’s only landlocked country, boasts a huge energy surplus, as its rivers and mountainous terrain supported a government-led push to build hydroelectric dams as a core economic pillar. The country currently exports about 80% of its electricity to other Asian countries like Thailand, China, and Singapore.
“They have plenty of land and a lot of water,” Kromadit says, adding that it has “the best natural conditions” for industrial development. (While Laos generates over 12 GW of capacity from over 80 hydro plants, most cross-border transmission lines bypass local communities, sticking consumers with frequent blackouts.)
To Kromadit, Laos’s potential is also backed by China, long the country’s top foreign investor. In 2025, China pumped $18 billion into Laos’s economy, primarily toward industry, mining, and agriculture, according to the Vientiane Times, a local newspaper.
Laos has been slotted into “China plus one” supply chains, where both Chinese and global manufacturers move some—or all—of their production to other countries, both to reduce cost and avoid tariffs on Chinese-origin products.
“China is the largest manufacturer of all products, so they can’t just keep building only within their country,” Kromadit explains. “They’re also being hit by political pressure from the U.S.”
After graduating from National Taiwan University with a degree in mechanical engineering, he returned to Thailand in 1975 and founded V&K Enterprise, an import-export business that focused on agricultural products, minerals, and seafood. But by the 1980s, he was frustrated with being “just a middleman.”
“I wanted to make more money,” Kromadit confesses. “When I was in the food business, even though I was the one who created all the channels and brought in business, once companies achieved success, they kicked me out.”
In 1988, he cofounded the Bang Pakong Industrial Estate on the eastern coast of Bangkok, then established Amata Corporation in 1989. Amata’s first industrial facility, Amata City Chon Buri, opened that same year.
After Kromadit visited Vietnam in 1990, he decided to make the country Amata’s first overseas market. “I found that the Vietnamese were focused, capable, and smart,” he says. “I thought that Vietnam, in the future, would compete with Thailand for industrial investments.” Amata launched Amata City Bien Hoa in Dong Nai province in 1994.
His prediction has largely come true: Vietnam is now Southeast Asia’s fastest-growing economy, with Q3 GDP growth of 9.95%. Hanoi wants to have Vietnam reach high-income status by 2045.
Amata today hosts more than 1,500 factories in 12 locations across Thailand, Vietnam, and Laos. It briefly attempted an expansion into Myanmar in 2019, with a facility in Yangon, the country’s commercial center. Plans were halted in early 2021 following a military coup and resulting civil war.
Amata positions its facilities as industrial cities that include not just factories but also housing, schools, hospitals, and shopping malls. The company’s flagship Chon Buri campus, for instance, houses the massive 38,000-square-meter Lotus Plus Mall, which includes a hypermarket, retail stores, banks, restaurants, and an international cinema.
The company’s facilities include kindergartens, schools, and technical training institutes, with more on the way. “We’re now looking to build a university,” Kromadit says.
Asked whether Amata might expand into other Southeast Asian markets, like Indonesia or Cambodia, Kromadit says the company already has enough land to occupy him for the rest of his life.
“The land that we have on hand is around 700 square kilometers,” he says. “It’s big enough to make me busy until I go to heaven.”

high_priority_articles.title: Why Is the US Stock Market Mixed Today (October 12)? Dow Jones Gains 0.4%, S&P 500 Slips 0.1% & Nasdaq Falls 0.3% as Oil Prices Surge and Fed Rate Hike Bets Weigh; Check What Investors Should Know - The Sunday Guardian
high_priority_articles.summary: Why Is the US Stock Market Mixed Today (October 12)? Dow Jones Gains 0.4%, S&P 500 Slips 0.1% & Nasdaq Falls 0.3% as Oil Prices Surge and Fed Rate Hike Bets Weigh; Check What Investors Should Know  The Sunday Guardian
high_priority_articles.full_text:
US Stock Market Mixed Today (October 12): The US stock market ended mixed on Monday, October 12, 2026, as rising crude oil prices, geopolitical uncertainty and concerns about inflation kept investors cautious. The Dow Jones Industrial Average advanced 0.4%, gaining around 215 points, while the S&P 500 slipped 0.1% and the Nasdaq Composite declined 0.3%, according to the Associated Press (AP).
US Stock Market Mixed Today
The mixed performance reflected a divide between sectors benefiting from higher energy prices and technology stocks facing pressure. Investors were also preparing for a busy week of corporate earnings and fresh US economic data that could influence expectations for the Federal Reserve’s next interest-rate decision.
Dow Jones Today
The Dow Jones Industrial Average outperformed the other major US stock indexes on Monday, rising 0.4%, or approximately 215 points. Gains in selected blue-chip companies helped the index advance despite uncertainty surrounding oil prices and the economic outlook.
According to Reuters, Salesforce shares were among the contributors to the Dow’s strength after an analyst upgrade, while energy stocks also benefited from higher crude prices. However, the gains were not broad enough to lift the entire market, as investors continued to assess the impact of higher energy costs on inflation and corporate earnings.
S&P 500 Today
The S&P 500 declined 0.1% as gains in energy and selected communication services stocks were offset by weakness elsewhere. The benchmark index remained close to its recent record levels, but the modest decline indicated that investors were reluctant to make aggressive bets ahead of key economic releases and quarterly earnings reports.
The broader market faced competing forces: higher oil prices supported energy companies but also raised concerns about business expenses, household spending and the possibility that inflation could remain elevated for longer.
Nasdaq Today
The Nasdaq Composite fell 0.3%, underperforming the Dow as technology stocks faced pressure. Higher energy costs and elevated bond yields can weigh on growth-oriented companies because they may increase operating expenses and reduce the present value investors assign to future earnings.
Investors are also watching technology companies’ earnings and spending plans, particularly as markets continue to assess the sustainability of the artificial intelligence investment boom. The Nasdaq’s decline, however, does not by itself indicate a broader collapse in technology shares.
Why Is the US Stock Market Mixed Today?
1. Oil Prices Surge Above $106 a Barrel
Rising crude oil prices were a major factor shaping Monday’s trading. Reuters reported that Brent crude futures climbed above $106 a barrel, reaching their highest levels in about two weeks amid geopolitical concerns following strikes on Riyadh’s international airport over the weekend.
The increase in oil prices supported energy shares but created uncertainty for the wider market. More expensive crude can raise transportation, manufacturing and fuel costs, potentially putting additional pressure on consumers and businesses. If these costs feed into inflation, the Federal Reserve could have less room to lower interest rates.
Oil prices remain sensitive to developments in the Middle East, particularly the conflict involving the US and Iran and the risks it poses to energy supplies and shipping routes.
2. Inflation Concerns Keep Investors Cautious
Investors are closely monitoring whether rising energy costs could reverse progress on inflation. Higher petrol, diesel and transportation prices can affect a wide range of goods and services, making the trajectory of consumer prices an important consideration for markets.
The Associated Press reported that investors are looking ahead to fresh US inflation figures and retail sales data this week. These releases could provide further clues about consumer demand and the extent to which higher energy costs are affecting the economy.
A stronger-than-expected inflation reading could reinforce concerns that interest rates may remain elevated for longer. Conversely, signs of easing price pressures could help support expectations for a less restrictive monetary policy.
3. Federal Reserve Rate Expectations Remain in Focus
The Federal Reserve’s interest-rate outlook is another important factor for Wall Street. When inflation remains persistent, policymakers may be more cautious about cutting borrowing costs. Higher interest rates can increase financing expenses for companies and households while making bonds more competitive with equities.
Reuters reported that markets were watching the upcoming inflation data and corporate earnings for clues about the economic outlook and the Fed’s next steps. Although interest-rate expectations can shift quickly as new information emerges, Monday’s mixed trading does not establish that the Fed will raise rates at its next meeting.
Investors should distinguish between market pricing, analyst expectations and an actual policy decision by the central bank.
4. Bond Market Closure Limits One Source of Trading Signals
US bond trading was closed on Monday in observance of Columbus Day. This meant investors had fewer fresh signals from Treasury yields, which have recently been an important influence on stock valuations.
Bond yields matter because they affect borrowing costs and the returns available from fixed-income investments. When yields rise, some investors may become less willing to pay high valuations for stocks, particularly companies whose expected profits lie further in the future.
With the bond market closed, investors had to assess other indicators, including oil prices, company-specific developments and expectations for the week’s economic releases.
What Economic Data and Earnings Should Investors Watch This Week?
The market’s attention is turning to two major developments: inflation data and the start of another round of corporate earnings reports.
Investors are expected to monitor consumer and producer price figures, retail sales and other economic indicators for signs of whether inflation is easing and whether consumer spending remains resilient. The data could influence expectations for interest rates and the outlook for corporate profitability.
Major US banks, including JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup and Wells Fargo, are scheduled to report quarterly results. Their earnings and commentary could provide insight into lending activity, consumer finances, investment banking and the broader health of the US economy.
Technology and other large-cap companies will also remain in focus as investors assess revenue growth, profit margins and spending on artificial intelligence. Strong results could support stocks, while weaker guidance or higher costs could add to volatility.
US Stock Market Today: What Should Investors Know?
Monday’s trading shows that the major US indexes can move in different directions when investors are balancing energy-sector gains against concerns about inflation, interest rates and technology valuations. The Dow’s advance does not mean the entire market rallied, just as the S&P 500 and Nasdaq declines do not necessarily signal a broad market sell-off. The relatively modest percentage changes suggest a mixed session rather than a decisive market move.
Investors should watch the incoming inflation data, earnings announcements, oil prices and changes in Treasury yields for clearer signals about the market’s next direction. Individual stocks may also react differently depending on their exposure to energy costs, interest rates and consumer demand.

high_priority_articles.title: 'FTAs can add $170 billion to India's GDP by 2035, cushion US tariffs' - Business Standard
high_priority_articles.summary: 'FTAs can add $170 billion to India's GDP by 2035, cushion US tariffs'  Business Standard
high_priority_articles.full_text:
'FTAs can add $170 billion to India's GDP by 2035, cushion US tariffs'
Bloomberg Economics estimates that India's expanding trade agreements could lift GDP by up to 2.1 per cent by 2035, while stronger exports elsewhere help offset US tariffs
Listen to This Article
India’s expanding network of free trade agreements (FTAs) could add $140-170 billion to its GDP by 2035, according to a report released by Bloomberg Economics on Monday.
“Our analysis suggests FTAs already in force should raise India’s GDP by 1.2 per cent by 2035 relative to baseline, rising to 1.7 per cent if the EU (European Union) and New Zealand agreements are implemented from 2027, a gain of about $140 billion at constant 2025 US dollars,” the report said.
Bloomberg Economics further said a US deal would add 0.2 percentage points, and if negotiations with the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) and Israel conclude over the next few years, the gain could rise by another 0.2 percentage points, leaving GDP 2.1 per cent higher (about $170 billion) by 2035.
The report said the Indian economy is well placed to absorb disruptions from the imposition of American tariffs, as expanding free trade partnerships aid the discovery of new markets, foreign direct investment and productivity gains, while global capital flows become more concentrated.
Bloomberg Economics estimated that the average tariff on Indian goods sold to the US has risen to 11.6 per cent from 2.4 per cent in 2024. “By 2035, we estimate the tariffs will cut Indian goods exports to the US by about one-fifth. But the hit to India’s economy should be limited. Less than 2 per cent of its output relies on US markets, and stronger exports elsewhere should cushion the blow. We estimate the effect on gross domestic product will be negligible,” the report said.
Also Read
Facing such uncertainty in its single largest export destination amid supply chain disruptions from the West Asian conflict, India is in negotiations with at least eight to nine more groups of countries and individual nations that together account for another $15 trillion of GDP, according to Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal. India has concluded nine free trade agreements (FTAs) with 38 developed countries in the past four and a half years. These nine agreements cover economies with a combined GDP of $60 trillion and 38 developed countries, Goyal said earlier.
The report projected India’s growth rates for calendar years 2026 and 2027 at 6.9 per cent and 7.4 per cent, respectively. Inflation is projected to rise from 2.2 per cent in 2025 to 4.5 per cent in 2026 and 5.3 per cent in 2027. The central bank's repo rate is forecast at 5.50 per cent for 2026 and 5.75 per cent in 2027, from 5.25 per cent in 2025.
The report further forecast that trade volumes, including imports, would rise even faster on completion of such agreements, with a rise of around 10 per cent by 2035 over 2024. “Imports would also climb as households and businesses gain access to new products and services, and manufacturers become more integrated into global value chains,” the report said.
However, the report noted that global capital flows are becoming more concentrated and more political, with flows between rival nations estimated to be 40 per cent lower than between allies, as capital zeroes in on artificial intelligence (AI) and semiconductors. The report said AI could boost India's GDP growth by 0.4–0.9 percentage points annually through higher factor productivity.

high_priority_articles.title: Ten casualties to one, by a NATO official’s count: Russia’s September in Ukraine’s kill zones - Euromaidan Press
high_priority_articles.summary: Ten casualties to one, by a NATO official’s count: Russia’s September in Ukraine’s kill zones  Euromaidan Press
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Russia suffered vastly more casualties than Ukraine in September, a senior NATO military official told Bloomberg. Ukraine’s General Staff put the month’s Russian toll only slightly lower.
September’s toll lands on a recruitment system that was already falling short. Ukraine’s military intelligence (HUR) estimated that Russian losses outran new contracts in June and July, when monthly losses ran lower. In August, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, citing military intelligence, warned that Russia is preparing a mass call-up after its parliamentary elections. That vote ended on 20 September.
Where the numbers come from
Russian casualties passed 50,000 in September, up to 28,000 of them killed, the official said. Ukraine’s losses over the same month came to about 5,000, according to the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity. Russia does not release casualty figures, Bloomberg noted. In late August, Pavlo Palisa, deputy head of Ukraine’s Presidential Office, put Russia’s July losses at 43,000 killed and wounded. Bloomberg could not confirm his figures.
To push forward, Russia keeps feeding troops into “kill zones,” the official said. These are stretches of ground saturated with armed drones, mines, and artillery fire. Maksym, call sign Rumyn, is a deputy company commander in the 46th Airmobile Brigade’s drone battalion. In April, he said the zone once ran 3–5 km deep and is now several times larger.
Ukraine suffered 10 times fewer casualties than Russia in Vivaldi counteroffensive, veteran says. Ukraine’s innovations in drone and ground robot tactics are changing frontline warfare
Rising stakes for Moscow
Russia’s defense spending is expected to near $199 billion this year, Bloomberg reported, citing two sources close to the government. That is about 40% above the plan the government set in late 2025.
Russian President Vladimir Putin would struggle to wind down the invasion without a political cost, Martin Jäger said last week. He heads Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service (BND).

high_priority_articles.title: ‘We still love you’: NATO envoy seeks to reassure Europe over US military pullback - AOL.co.uk
high_priority_articles.summary: ‘We still love you’: NATO envoy seeks to reassure Europe over US military pullback  AOL.co.uk
high_priority_articles.full_text:
US Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker told European Commissioner for Defence Andrius Kubilius that Washington remains committed to Europe’s defence, amid an ongoing US military review withdrawing thousands of troops and key strategic assets from the continent.
“We still love you,” Whitaker said at the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday in the Polish capital.
“I keep telling our European allies… the United States isn't stepping back.”
His remarks came during a panel on NATO 3.0 — a US-backed model that calls for Europe to take the lead with its conventional defences as American forces draw down from the continent and shift their attention elsewhere.
Kubilius said NATO 3.0 did not mean the United States was saying, “We don’t love you anymore, Europeans, so you should do your own job”. Rather, he argued, Europe needed to develop the capabilities to deter aggression on its own territory.
“Europe needs to take responsibility in our hands,” he said.
Kubilius has previously estimated that replacing US strategic military assets could cost Europe up to €500 billion. Experts have also suggested that Europe could need 300,000 additional troops to defend itself against Russia in a scenario in which Washington continues to withdraw its military support.
Since Donald Trump returned to the White House, Washington has sought to redirect military resources towards other regions, including the Indo-Pacific, to counter China’s growing influence.
The Pentagon’s review of US military deployments in Europe is expected to conclude by December, with its findings to be presented to US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth. The assessment could pave the way for further reductions in America’s military presence on the continent.
However, separate force reductions are already under way. In May, for example, the Pentagon ordered the withdrawal of approximately 5,000 troops from Germany and cancelled a planned deployment of a long-range fires battalion.
Whitaker said he did not want to “preview” further measures under the review because “it is not ready”, but argued that Washington’s push for a more European NATO was “working”.
“The proof is in where we're sitting today, here in Poland, spending 4.7% on core defence and leading really the alliance to a stronger, more capable military,” he said.
Allies agreed to raise their core defence spending target from 2% to 3.5% of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2035 at the 2025 NATO summit in The Hague, alongside a further 1.5% for broader security and defence spending.
"That is what the United States is expecting from all of its allies," Whitaker said of the overall 5% defence spending target.
Poland is among NATO’s highest spenders on core defence as a share of GDP, according to the alliance’s latest estimates.
The effort to increase defence spending also comes as the European Union seeks to strengthen its military capabilities by 2030, amid warnings from European intelligence agencies that Russia could pose a more direct threat to NATO in the coming years.
But the rearmament drive is facing significant hurdles. A leaked version of the European Defence Agency's landmark report — aiming to assess the progress — reveals major capability gaps, most notably in drone defences and maritime warfare.

high_priority_articles.title: Fed minutes: Another rate hike likely coming this year to combat persistent inflation - ABC11 News
high_priority_articles.summary: Fed minutes: Another rate hike likely coming this year to combat persistent inflation  ABC11 News
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Federal Reserve officials are expecting another interest rate increase in 2026.
WASHINGTON, D.C. -- Most Federal Reserve officials expect that another interest rate increase will likely be needed this year to combat inflation, according to minutes released Wednesday from the central bank’s most recent meeting.
The officials unanimously agreed that inflation was still elevated and had not made much progress toward their 2% target in recent months, the minutes said. The Fed increased its key interest rate at the Sept. 15-16 meeting by a quarter-point to about 3.9%, its first increase in three years.
The increase defied President Donald Trump’s repeated calls for the Fed to cut rates and prompted the president to criticize the Fed’s rate-setting committee, though he still expressed support for Chairman Kevin Warsh, whom he appointed earlier this year. The rate increase comes as Americans are already struggling with high costs for groceries, gas, and housing, and as affordability has taken on a leading role in the upcoming midterm elections, just seven weeks away.
Longer-term interest rates for mortgages and other borrowing have also jumped in the past few months for a range of reasons, including rising government debt, heavy borrowing by tech firms to finance data center construction, climbing oil and gas prices, and signs that growth and inflation remain elevated. The Fed’s rate hike has likely played only a limited role in the increase.
Still, key policymakers have said since the meeting that the Fed can take some time to monitor the economy and the impact of last month’s rate hike before making another move. Wall Street investors now forecast the Fed will keep its rate unchanged at its next meeting Oct. 28-29, according to futures pricing, and raise it when they meet in December.
Philip Jefferson, vice chair of the Fed’s board of governors, said last week that policymakers “will need to come to our own judgment, which may take more time.”
Inflation, according to the Fed’s preferred measure, came in lower than many economists expected in August but remained elevated. Overall prices rose 3.4% compared with a year earlier, while core prices — which exclude volatile food and energy categories — increased 3%. On a monthly basis, prices rose 0.3% from July to August, and core prices just 0.2%.
According to the minutes, even with the rise in longer-term rates, many officials said that financial conditions—which includes rising stock prices — “appeared to be supportive of economic growth,” a sign that more rate hikes may be needed to cool the economy.
Several policymakers said that they saw the Fed’s rate as too low to restrain the economy, or only acting as a mild restraint. That suggests they would support multiple rate hikes to rein in inflation.
Higher oil and gas prices stemming from the Iran war and the lingering effects of tariffs have lifted costs in recent months. But even excluding those trends, many Fed officials believe inflation is stuck between 2.5% and 3%, above its target. Spiking prices for semiconductors, computer equipment, and electrical components due to the rapid surge in data center construction have also played a big role in accelerating inflation.
The Fed lifted its key interest rate to about 3.9% at its Sept. 15-16 meeting, its first increase in three years. Higher rates are intended to slow borrowing and spending, cool the economy, and bring down inflation.
Warsh emphasized after the announcement that the economy has shown signs of gathering speed since the central bank decided to keep rates unchanged in late July.
“The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Warsh said at a news conference after last month’s meeting. “We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective clearly and at sufficient speed. Today the FOMC decided that this standard has not been satisfied,” he added, referring to the policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee, an arm of the Fed.
Trump criticized the committee for voting to raise rates, calling them “very political,” but he did not single out Warsh.
“They’re raising rates to make Trump do as bad as they can possibly do,” the president said.

(Kitco NewsWire) – The gold market is struggling to maintain its recent recovery as persistent inflation pressures, elevated bond yields and a U.S. dollar trading near an 18-month high continue to create significant headwinds for the precious metal ahead of another critical week of economic data.
Gold prices started the week with modest gains, briefly trading above $4,200 an ounce during the Asian session; however, bullish momentum has faded as investors remain reluctant to take significant positions ahead of Wednesday's U.S. Consumer Price Index report.
Spot gold was last quoted around $4,156.20 an ounce ahead of the North American trading session, down nearly 1% on the day. The precious metal has been unable to build on last week's recovery after prices briefly fell below $4,100 an ounce. Despite the recent buying momentum, gold remains well below its August highs as investors continue to assess the implications of tighter monetary policy and stubborn inflation.
Silver is also struggling to maintain its recovery, with prices trading around $60.35 an ounce after briefly pushing above $61 earlier in the session.
The latest U.S. economic data continues to paint a complicated picture for financial markets as weakening consumer confidence contrasts with persistently elevated inflation expectations.
On Friday, the University of Michigan reported that its preliminary consumer sentiment index fell to 46.3 in October, down from 48.1 in September and below expectations of 47.6. The current economic conditions index dropped sharply to 44.7, its lowest reading on record.
At the same time, consumers' one-year inflation expectations increased to 4.7%, up from 4.6%, while longer-term expectations rose to 3.5% from 3.4%.
The disappointing sentiment data follows September's weaker-than-expected employment report, which showed that the U.S. economy created only 29,000 jobs, while the unemployment rate increased to 4.2%. Although signs of slowing economic growth would normally support expectations for looser monetary policy, persistent inflation pressures continue to complicate the Federal Reserve's outlook.
Market positioning remains tilted toward further monetary tightening, with interest rate futures reflecting roughly an 85% probability of at least one additional rate hike by December. Investors see only about a 17% chance of a rate increase at the October meeting. The divergence between slowing employment growth and elevated inflation expectations is keeping Treasury yields and the U.S. dollar supported, limiting gold's ability to sustain its recent recovery.
The U.S. dollar remains a significant obstacle for the precious metal, with the U.S. Dollar Index holding near 102.20, close to its highest level in approximately 18 months. (Kitco Global Index shows how much of today's gold move is the dollar versus the gold market itself.)
Simon-Peter Massabni, Head of Business Development at XS.com, said that the dollar continues to benefit from the combination of persistent energy inflation, geopolitical uncertainty and elevated U.S. Treasury yields.
Massabni added that persistent inflation pressures are preventing central banks from easing monetary policy and forcing fixed-income markets to adjust to expectations for higher interest rates.
Although the dollar's strength is weighing on gold, analysts note that the precious metal continues to attract safe-haven interest as investors navigate deteriorating economic conditions and growing geopolitical uncertainty.
The ongoing conflict between the United States and Iran remains a significant source of uncertainty, particularly as negotiations to reopen the Strait of Hormuz have failed to produce a lasting resolution. Iranian officials have rejected U.S. proposals as inadequate, while renewed attacks on Saudi Arabian infrastructure and continued military deployments have raised concerns about further regional escalation. Although oil prices have eased following President Donald Trump's announcement of a proposed energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, the risk of renewed disruptions to Middle Eastern energy supplies remains elevated. Brent crude has retreated toward $105 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate is trading above $92 a barrel. For gold, the conflict remains a double-edged sword: geopolitical uncertainty supports safe-haven demand, but higher energy prices threaten to keep inflation elevated, reinforcing expectations for tighter monetary policy.
Meanwhile, the U.S. bond market continues to present another significant challenge for gold as the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield remains well above 5%, near levels not seen in almost two decades. Although rising yields increase the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding assets such as gold, analysts note that the reasons behind the bond market's weakness are becoming increasingly important. With U.S. sovereign debt exceeding $40 trillion and annual interest costs surpassing $1 trillion, investors are demanding greater compensation for the risks associated with holding long-term government debt. Persistent inflation, growing borrowing requirements and concerns about the sustainability of U.S. fiscal policy are contributing to higher term premiums. While these developments create immediate headwinds for gold, they could also reinforce its longer-term appeal as an alternative monetary asset and portfolio diversification tool.
Massabni said that despite the current headwinds, gold is approaching an important technical and fundamental turning point.
"The key question is not simply whether gold can rebound from this area, but whether the underlying economic and fundamental conditions are strong enough to turn a potential recovery into a more sustainable bullish trend," he said.
He identified the area between $4,155 and $4,177 an ounce as an important support zone, adding that a sustained recovery will depend on whether inflation data allows Treasury yields and the U.S. dollar to lose momentum.
However, he warned that stronger-than-expected inflation could reinforce expectations for additional monetary tightening, potentially exposing gold to renewed selling pressure.
The market's next major test will come Wednesday with the release of September's Consumer Price Index. Investors will be watching whether rising energy prices are becoming embedded in broader inflation pressures, particularly core consumer prices.
A softer-than-expected inflation report could ease expectations for further Federal Reserve rate hikes, providing some relief for gold and silver. Conversely, another upside inflation surprise could push bond yields and the dollar higher, increasing the risk of renewed selling pressure across the precious metals complex.
Gold's near-term outlook remains bearish as prices continue to trade below a descending trendline and longer-term moving averages. Initial support is seen at $4,175.03 an ounce, followed by $4,141.86 and $4,103.24. A break below these levels could expose further downside toward $4,067.42. On the upside, initial resistance is seen at $4,226.82, with a sustained break above that level potentially opening the door to $4,271.57 and $4,311.17. Analysts note that gold will need to overcome its declining trendline to establish a more sustainable bullish recovery.
Meanwhile, silver's technical outlook also remains cautious as the precious metal struggles to overcome resistance from its declining trendline. Analysts are watching initial support at $59.96 an ounce, followed by $58.74 and $57.64. On the upside, initial resistance is seen at $61.72, followed by $63.06 and $65.09. A sustained move above $61.72 would be an important indication of improving bullish momentum, while a break below $59.96 could signal renewed selling pressure.
Although precious metals remain vulnerable to further near-term volatility, underlying investment demand continues to provide some support. Global gold-backed exchange-traded funds attracted approximately $10 billion in September, with holdings rising to a record 4,256 tonnes. Central bank demand also remains elevated, with official-sector purchases projected at approximately 720 tonnes this year.
With U.S. Treasury markets closed Monday for the Columbus Day holiday, trading conditions could remain relatively subdued as investors wait for fresh inflation data and further clarity on the Federal Reserve's monetary policy outlook.

high_priority_articles.title: ASML vs. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026? - The Motley Fool
high_priority_articles.summary: ASML vs. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?  The Motley Fool
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Demand for advanced computing power links two of the chip industry's best-known companies. ASML Holding (ASML -1.69%) makes the lithography systems that chipmakers use to print circuits on silicon, and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM -1.98%), known as TSMC, is a contract manufacturer that makes chips for other companies.
The two also work together. In a joint release in September, ASML and TSMC said they had formed an initiative to move High NA EUV lithography to larger photomasks, and that TSMC intends to use ASML's High NA technology in high-volume manufacturing for advanced nodes starting in 2030.
Investors often compare them because their businesses are closely linked, even though their financial profiles differ.
ASML & TSM: Performance Comparison
Key Financial Metrics
The case for ASML
ASML supplies chipmakers with lithography systems and related software and services used to print circuit patterns on silicon wafers. Its flagship products include Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV) and Deep Ultraviolet (DUV) machines used to produce advanced chips. ASML says it is currently the world's only manufacturer of EUV lithography systems. According to ASML's 2025 annual report, four customers accounted for about 61% of ASML's 2025 net sales.
ASML reports its results in euros, and the annual figures here are approximate conversions to U.S. dollars. In 2025, revenue reached nearly $36.6 billion, up roughly 15.6% from the previous year. The company reported net income of about $10.8 billion for the period, resulting in a net margin of nearly 29.4%.
For the quarter ended June 28, 2026, ASML reported net sales of 9.3 billion euros and a gross margin of 54%. In July, it raised its 2026 outlook to total net sales of 43-45 billion euros.
Based on its December 2025 balance sheet, ASML's debt-to-equity ratio, calculated from total debt and shareholders' equity, is about 0.2x. This ratio compares total debt to shareholders' equity, indicating modest borrowing relative to shareholders' equity.
The current ratio, also calculated from the balance sheet, measures the ability to pay short-term obligations with assets expected to convert to cash within a year, and is roughly 1.3x. Free cash flow, which ASML calculates as operating cash flow minus purchases of property, plant, and equipment and intangible assets, was approximately $12.4 billion for the year.
The case for Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing
TSMC operates as a pure-play foundry, meaning it manufactures chips for customers rather than designing its own. In 2025, it manufactured 12,682 products for 534 customers, with demand coming from markets such as high-performance computing and smartphones. Advanced technologies at 7 nanometers and below accounted for 74% of its 2025 wafer revenue.
TSMC reports its results in New Taiwan dollars, and the annual figures here are approximate conversions to U.S. dollars.
In 2025, revenue reached roughly $121.3 billion, up about 31.6% in New Taiwan dollars and 35.9% in U.S. dollars, according to TSMC. The company earned net income of about $54.7 billion, for a net margin of approximately 45.1%.
For the quarter ended June 30, 2026, TSMC reported revenue up 36% year over year in New Taiwan dollars, with a gross margin of 67.7%.
Based on TSMC's December 2025 balance sheet, I calculate a current ratio of roughly 2.5x to 2.6x, depending on which of TSMC's year-end statements is used. That means current assets are about two and a half times current liabilities.
The debt-to-equity ratio, calculated as interest-bearing debt divided by total equity, is approximately 0.2x, a modest level of debt relative to shareholder equity. Free cash flow, calculated by subtracting capital expenditures from operating cash flow, reached about NT$1.0 trillion, or approximately $32 billion at the converted rate, for the fiscal year.
Risk profile comparison
ASML's customer concentration is a risk, since a change in spending plans at any one of its four largest customers can move its results. Because its customers are chipmakers that decide when to add capacity, a slowdown in industry spending would reduce demand for its systems.
Export controls are another factor. ASML's annual report says, "Changes in export controls may have a material impact on our business for example on the sales volume, mix and timing," and China accounted for about 29% of its 2025 net sales in the geographic breakdown of its annual report.
According to its interim report, which attributes sales to the location of customers' facilities, China's share fell to about 16% of net sales in the first half of 2026.
TSMC's business requires heavy, continuing investment in factories and technology, with capital expenditures of about $40.9 billion in 2025, according to TSMC. Geopolitical risk is the other main concern, since the majority of its principal production facilities are in Taiwan. TSMC also faces competition from other foundries, including Intel (INTC -3.20%), which TSMC's chief executive described as a formidable competitor on the April 2026 earnings call, and Samsung Electronics (SSNLF +0.00%), which TrendForce estimates ranked second in foundry revenue in the second quarter of 2026.
TSMC's customer base is also concentrated at the top, as its annual report shows two customers accounted for 19% and 17% of 2025 net revenue. Demand for TSMC's chips also depends on its customers' end markets, including smartphones and consumer electronics, so weakness in those categories would affect sales.
Valuation comparison
TSMC has the lower forward P/E of the two in the table, and the two companies are close on price-to-sales. The P/S ratio measures a company's market value against its past twelve months of sales. The forward P/E compares the stock price to future earnings estimates.
| Metric | ASML | Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing | 
|---|---|---|
| Forward P/E | 42.8x | 28.0x | 
| P/S ratio | 18.2x | 17.5x | 
Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
While TSMC looks like the better buy to me, I'd be a patient buyer, as shares of both companies have risen sharply over the past year and TSMC's production is concentrated in Taiwan.
My reasoning starts with the fact that each business depends on its customers. Both are concentrated.
TSMC's two largest customers accounted for about 36% of its 2025 net revenue, according to its annual report, and four customers accounted for about 61% of ASML's 2025 net sales. TSMC also serves 534 customers in total, so the business has a broader base beyond its largest accounts. ASML says it is currently the world's only manufacturer of EUV lithography systems, which is a strong foundation, though it also means a handful of chipmakers shape demand.
TSMC also carries the lower forward earnings multiple in the table, which adds to its appeal for me.
If I were buying, I'd start with a modest TSMC position and add to it over time, planning to hold for years. Sharp pullbacks can happen with both stocks, and if the business still looked sound after one, I'd treat it as a chance to add more.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
New Delhi: India's free trade agreements (FTAs) already in force, along with those agreed with the European Union (EU) and New Zealand, could add about $140 billion to the country's gross domestic product (GDP) by 2035, lifting economic output by 1.7% and export volumes by 6.2% compared with a baseline without the trade deals, according to a Bloomberg Economics report.
The October 2026 report, titled Silicon, Steel and Statecraft: New Economic Thinking for the New Economy Forum said the projected gain assumes that the agreements with the EU and New Zealand are implemented from 2027. The $140 billion estimate is expressed in constant 2025 US dollars.
The gains could increase to about $170 billion, or 2.1% of GDP, by 2035 if India reaches an interim trade agreement with the US and concludes ongoing negotiations with the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) and Israel over the next few years, the report estimated.
According to Bloomberg Economics, FTAs already in force could increase India's GDP by 1.2% and export volumes by 4% by 2035, compared with the baseline. The addition of the EU and New Zealand agreements would increase the estimated gains to 1.7% and 6.2%, respectively.
A proposed interim agreement with the US could add another 0.2 percentage point to GDP gains, taking the total to 1.9%, while export volumes could increase by 7.8% compared with the baseline. The conclusion of negotiations with the EAEU, GCC and Israel could raise the projected GDP gain to 2.1% and export volumes to 9.2%.
The estimates are based on a computable general equilibrium model developed by the World Trade Organization. The report's baseline assumes that US tariffs remain at their 2024 levels and none of the trade agreements are implemented.
Bloomberg Economics said that the average US tariff on Indian goods had increased to 11.6% in August 2026 from 2.4% in 2024. It estimated that tariffs at these levels would reduce Indian goods exports to the US by about one-fifth by 2035.
However, the report estimated that the impact on India's overall GDP would be negligible, as less than 2% of the country's output depends on US markets and stronger exports elsewhere could cushion the impact.
The report noted that the average US tariff rate across trading partners stood at 10.7% in August, compared with 2.3% in 2024. Tariffs at this level could reduce US goods imports by roughly 15% compared with the previous regime.
The report said that agreements with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), the UK and Oman entered into force during 2025-26, adding to agreements with Australia and the United Arab Emirates that took effect in 2022. India also signed an FTA with New Zealand and concluded negotiations with the EU.
Bloomberg Economics modelled the impact of these agreements through changes in bilateral tariffs, reductions in non-tariff barriers and productivity gains associated with higher foreign direct investment.
For its calculations, the report assumed that India's trade partners eliminate tariffs on Indian goods in the first year, while India eliminates tariffs on industrial products and halves tariffs on agricultural products over a phased implementation period.
It also assumed that the cost of non-tariff measures on goods and services declines gradually by 25% over 15 years, alongside additional reductions in barriers affecting services.
The model incorporated investment commitments of $100 billion over 15 years under the EFTA agreement, of which roughly $35 billion was expected to be additional, and $20 billion under the New Zealand agreement, almost all of which was expected to be additional.
Beyond trade agreements, the report examined how domestic reforms could increase India's economic gains.
It estimated that a further improvement in manufacturing efficiency, modelled as a roughly 2% reduction in production costs, could add about 0.5 percentage point to GDP gains and roughly 1 percentage point to export gains by 2035.
The report also highlighted the potential benefits of moving workers from agriculture into manufacturing and services. More than 40% of India's workforce remains in agriculture, with high underemployment, it said.
A scenario involving higher agricultural productivity, phased in over a decade and allowing workers to move into manufacturing and services, could add about 2 percentage points to GDP gains and slightly more than 1 percentage point to export growth.
Bloomberg Economics said that realising the benefits of FTAs would require effective implementation, continued domestic reforms, reliable access to energy, critical minerals and advanced technologies, and measures to unlock the potential of India's workforce.

The British Pound (GBP) trades marginally lower against the Japanese Yen (JPY) at around 209.25 during the late Asian trade on Tuesday. The cross faces mild selling pressure even as Bank of England (BoE) policymaker Megan Greene has argued in favor that the central bank should act now to contain inflationary pressures before it gets too late and it starts spreading to wages and broad consumer prices.
So far this year, the BoE has kept interest rates steady at 3.75%. Meanwhile, market experts see the BoE raising interest rates in the November meeting on the back improved economic outlook.
Analysts at Commerzbank highlight that the UK economy has “remained relatively resilient so far this year,” noting that “following growth of 0.6% q/q in the first quarter, second-quarter GDP was revised up to 0.5% in the final release.” They add that “monthly GDP data for July, showing a 0.4% m/m increase, also point to a solid start to the third quarter,” reinforcing the picture of firmer underlying momentum.
Against this backdrop, Commerzbank argues that “the improved growth outlook should make it easier for the BoE to raise rates further in order to lean against inflation.” The bank acknowledges that “until now, we had not expected the BoE to hike rates again,” but says “recent developments… have led us to conclude that a November rate hike is now more likely than not.” Moreover, Commerzbank “do[es] not expect it to be a one-off move,” and now “anticipate[s] another hike in February, taking Bank Rate to 4.25%.”
For fresh cues regarding the UK economic strength, investors await monthly Gross Domestic Product (GDP) data for August, which is scheduled for Thursday. According to estimates, the UK economy contracted 0.1% in August after a 0.4% expansion in July.

Central banks FAQs
Central Banks have a key mandate which is making sure that there is price stability in a country or region. Economies are constantly facing inflation or deflation when prices for certain goods and services are fluctuating. Constant rising prices for the same goods means inflation, constant lowered prices for the same goods means deflation. It is the task of the central bank to keep the demand in line by tweaking its policy rate. For the biggest central banks like the US Federal Reserve (Fed), the European Central Bank (ECB) or the Bank of England (BoE), the mandate is to keep inflation close to 2%.
A central bank has one important tool at its disposal to get inflation higher or lower, and that is by tweaking its benchmark policy rate, commonly known as interest rate. On pre-communicated moments, the central bank will issue a statement with its policy rate and provide additional reasoning on why it is either remaining or changing (cutting or hiking) it. Local banks will adjust their savings and lending rates accordingly, which in turn will make it either harder or easier for people to earn on their savings or for companies to take out loans and make investments in their businesses. When the central bank hikes interest rates substantially, this is called monetary tightening. When it is cutting its benchmark rate, it is called monetary easing.
A central bank is often politically independent. Members of the central bank policy board are passing through a series of panels and hearings before being appointed to a policy board seat. Each member in that board often has a certain conviction on how the central bank should control inflation and the subsequent monetary policy. Members that want a very loose monetary policy, with low rates and cheap lending, to boost the economy substantially while being content to see inflation slightly above 2%, are called ‘doves’. Members that rather want to see higher rates to reward savings and want to keep a lit on inflation at all time are called ‘hawks’ and will not rest until inflation is at or just below 2%.
Normally, there is a chairman or president who leads each meeting, needs to create a consensus between the hawks or doves and has his or her final say when it would come down to a vote split to avoid a 50-50 tie on whether the current policy should be adjusted. The chairman will deliver speeches which often can be followed live, where the current monetary stance and outlook is being communicated. A central bank will try to push forward its monetary policy without triggering violent swings in rates, equities, or its currency. All members of the central bank will channel their stance toward the markets in advance of a policy meeting event. A few days before a policy meeting takes place until the new policy has been communicated, members are forbidden to talk publicly. This is called the blackout period.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
By JOSEPH KRAUSS
It’s been a year since a ceasefire deal brokered by U.S. President Donald Trump and Arab allies promised to end the war in Gaza, and Israel is still launching deadly strikes on the devastated territory.
The agreement halted major military operations, freed all remaining hostages and increased humanitarian access. But it has failed to deliver on promises of a new Palestinian administration aided by international forces, the disarmament of Hamas and an end to Israel’s control over more than half the territory. Almost nothing has been rebuilt.
Israel has tied any progress on the other issues to Hamas’ complete disarmament, while the militant group — and the Trump administration — say they should happen simultaneously. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hardened his stance over the summer, openly defying Trump, his most important ally, ahead of Israeli elections later this month.
The wrangling has left Gaza’s 2 million Palestinians in limbo. Most are sheltering in rodent-infested tent camps, the rubble of their former neighborhoods or war-damaged buildings at risk of collapse.
In the Jabaliya area of the northern Gaza Strip, Abdullah Abu Zubaida’s family lives in a makeshift shelter built from the debris of their house.
“When the ceasefire began last October, we expected the war to halt, assassinations to cease, and aid to flow in,” he said. None of that has happened.
For Ne’man Abu Jarad and his family, displaced from Beit Lahia in northern Gaza to Khan Younis in the south, the truce also has brought no clear path home. The family, including five daughters, continues to live in tents.
“The ceasefire is merely nominal, ink on paper,” Abu Jarad said.
Early success raised hopes of ending the war
The 20-point ceasefire agreement, reached after months of negotiations under the Biden and Trump administrations, ended major military operations and led to the return of all the remaining hostages taken in Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack that ignited the war.
Hamas fighters killed some 1,200 people that day and abducted 251. Israel responded with massive bombardment and a ground invasion that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.
The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, maintains detailed records and is seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It does not distinguish between civilians and militants in its toll but says women and children make up around half the dead.
After the deal was announced, Trump called for a new era of harmony in the Middle East. “We have a once-in-a-lifetime chance to put the old feuds and bitter hatreds behind us,” he said at a summit marking the deal.
The agreement called for much more
The agreement called for Hamas to hand over power to a committee of Palestinian administrators vetted by the Board of Peace, a new body chaired by Trump and charged with implementing the ceasefire.
Hamas officially dissolved their government in July but left the civil service intact and remain the dominant power in the roughly 40% of Gaza not controlled by the Israeli military. Israel has meanwhile barred the new Palestinian administration from entering Gaza via Egypt.
The formation of an International Stabilization Force was announced in February but has yet to materialize. Indonesia, which pledged the largest troop contingent — 8,000 soldiers — put those plans on hold last spring as the world’s focus shifted to the Iran war.
Israel was supposed to withdraw from Gaza but has instead seized more territory, pushing the so-called yellow Line of Control westward toward the Mediterranean Sea. It has also carried out regular strikes on individuals it accused of violating the ceasefire, approaching the yellow line or having taken part in the Oct. 7 attack — strikes that have often killed civilians.
Israeli strikes have killed over 1,400 Palestinians since the ceasefire took effect, according to the Gaza Health Ministry. Sporadic attacks have killed five Israeli soldiers in Gaza in the same period.
More deadlock after Netanyahu defied Trump
In July, Trump announced a deal to disarm Hamas, portraying it as a breakthrough in the long-stalled process.
That deal, an extension of the original ceasefire, called for Hamas to disarm “in a gradual, sequential and time-bound manner” that is “linked to an Israeli withdrawal, in phases.” Hamas confirmed for the first time that it had agreed to disarm, also linking it to Israel halting its strikes and withdrawing from Gaza.
Days later, Netanyahu announced that Israel would not withdraw from any part of Gaza until after Hamas has been completely disarmed, explicitly rejecting the agreement announced by Trump.
The rare instance of friction between the two allies came as Netanyahu seeks to shore up his nationalist base ahead of Oct. 27 elections that could end his nearly unbroken 17-year rule, the longest in Israel’s history.
Netanyahu has come under fire over security and intelligence failures leading up to the Oct. 7 attack, with opponents accusing him of having been soft on Hamas. That gives him little space to make even minor compromises on Gaza, at least until a new government is formed, which could take months.
In the meantime, virtually nothing has been rebuilt in Gaza, Hamas is weakened but still in power, and a return to fighting cannot be ruled out.
Associated Press journalist Wafaa Shurafa in Jabaliya, Gaza Strip, contributed to this report.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
Summary
Czech companies are seeking joint ventures, investment and technology partnerships in India, with the India–EU trade agreement expected to support deeper commercial ties. Czech minister Karel Havlíček outlined opportunities in engineering, construction, energy and transport during a business forum in New Delhi. The agreement is not yet in force.
Czech delegation looks beyond export sales
The India–EU FTA could create opportunities for Czech investment and joint ventures in India, according to Czech First Deputy Prime Minister and Industry and Trade Minister Karel Havlíček.
Addressing the CII-organised India–Czech Republic Business Forum in New Delhi on 12 October, Havlíček said Czech businesses were interested in establishing partnerships and investing locally alongside their export activities.
He identified construction, energy, transport and research and development as areas for cooperation. He also highlighted Czechia’s engineering capabilities, including aircraft manufacturing.
The minister linked the delegation’s interest in local partnerships with India’s manufacturing strategy. His remarks describe prospective business opportunities, rather than a quantified investment commitment or a confirmed portfolio of new projects.
Business mission covers three Indian centres
The forum forms part of a Czech business mission scheduled for 12–15 October, covering Delhi, Bengaluru and Mumbai.
Ahead of the visit, the Czech Ministry of Industry and Trade said the mission would support companies entering the Indian market and those seeking to expand existing operations.
The programme also included a planned roundtable with Invest India focused on developing bilateral investment opportunities. Direct business contacts and meetings were identified as important elements of the delegation’s approach.
The mission places the minister’s comments within a broader effort to develop commercial relationships. For participating companies, the immediate focus is identifying partners and market opportunities while the trade agreement progresses through its approval process.
The visit’s stated objectives combine market entry, business expansion and investment cooperation, extending the engagement beyond the promotion of finished-product exports alone.
Negotiations concluded, implementation still pending
India and the European Union concluded FTA negotiations on 27 January 2026. The European Commission subsequently put forward a proposal for a Council decision authorising signature.
Negotiating an agreement, signing it and bringing it into force are separate stages. The EU process requires the relevant Council decisions and European Parliament consent, while India must also complete its approval requirements.
Consequently, the agreement’s tariff preferences should be understood as forthcoming provisions, rather than benefits already available to shipments.
The talks began in 2007, were suspended in 2013 and resumed in 2022. Separate negotiations on investment protection and geographical indications were also launched alongside the renewed FTA process.
That distinction is relevant to the investment discussion: the trade agreement and the separate investment protection negotiations address related but different aspects of the commercial relationship.
Industrial tariff reductions underpin the opportunity
The negotiated agreement envisages eliminating or reducing tariffs on 96.6% of EU goods exports to India by value. The European Commission estimates eventual annual duty savings of approximately €4 billion for European products.
Industrial goods feature prominently. Tariffs on machinery, chemicals and pharmaceuticals are to be mostly eliminated, while automobile and component provisions include phased reductions.
These changes provide a commercial backdrop to Czech interest in engineering and industrial cooperation. Lower trade barriers could support cross-border equipment and component supply, although individual benefits will depend on product coverage and implementation schedules.
The agreement also includes provisions on intellectual property and services, including maritime transport. Such commitments extend its scope beyond merchandise tariffs and could support businesses combining technology, equipment and services.
The Commission’s projections concern the overall EU–India relationship; they do not establish a specific increase in Czech exports or investment.
Indian exporters also stand to gain
The agreement provides reciprocal opportunities for Indian businesses. India’s commerce ministry says more than 99% of Indian exports by trade value will gain preferential access to the EU.
Engineering goods, textiles, apparel, leather, footwear, marine products and other labour-intensive sectors are among the areas identified for improved access.
The framework also covers rules of origin, customs and trade facilitation, regulatory cooperation and technical barriers to trade. These provisions matter to manufacturers seeking to build supply relationships across the two markets.
For ports, freight forwarders and logistics providers, any resulting expansion in industrial trade could create additional demand for cargo movement. Its scale will depend on implementation and actual business decisions.
The Czech delegation’s engagement therefore represents an effort to develop partnerships ahead of the agreement’s application, with investment and manufacturing cooperation central to the discussion.
FAQs
What opportunities are Czech companies exploring?
Joint ventures, investment and cooperation in engineering, construction, energy, transport and research and development.
Who outlined these opportunities?
Czech First Deputy Prime Minister and Industry and Trade Minister Karel Havlíček.
Is the India–EU FTA already in force?
No. Negotiations have concluded, but the agreement must complete signature and approval procedures before taking effect.
Were specific Czech investment commitments announced?
The reported remarks did not provide a quantified investment package.
How could Indian exporters benefit?
The agreement envisages preferential EU market access across a broad range of Indian exports, subject to its provisions and implementation.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia's energy minister vowed a firm response Monday following a series of deadly Houthi attacks, acknowledging that the kingdom’s infrastructure and resilience have been tested.
The Houthi attacks over the weekend marked a sharp escalation in the Yemen war, where Saudi Arabia has long supported the internationally recognized government.
On Sunday, a strike hit Riyadh's international airport, killing one person, just hours after another Houthi-claimed attack on the same site killed 13 people and left hundreds of others wounded, forcing authorities to suspend operations there.
The attacks on Saudi Arabia, a regional powerhouse and the world's top oil exporter which has poured billions of dollars into its military, were the deadliest to hit the kingdom in a decade.
"For Saudi Arabia, these circumstances have tested our infrastructure, our institutions, our people, and our resilience. They have also tested decisions made long before present crises, because resilience is built before crises begin," Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said.
"Energy security can't be taken for granted," he told a high-profile conference in Riyadh. "The events of recent weeks are serious, our response must be equally serious."
The Houthis on Sunday claimed multiple attacks over the last 24 hours, including on the airport, and threatened to keep targeting the kingdom's transit hubs, calling them "a theater of operations for our forces."
Hours later, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the group reported that a projectile struck the capital's King Khalid International Airport, sparking a fire.
Air defenses also intercepted a missile nearby, it added. Journalists and locals reported hearing multiple blasts in the city Sunday.
"The whole house shook," said one resident of the Al-Aarid neighborhood in the city's north.
Authorities extended the suspension of operations at the airport, even as Saudi Arabia's high-profile convention and entertainment season kicks off this month.
Riyadh usually hosts a packed calendar of events, including its flagship investment conference drawing foreign leaders and business titans.
The airport was not the only one in the country to be targeted: the civil aviation authority also reported another attack on Dammam airport in the east.
The Saudi-led coalition said Monday it had also "intercepted and destroyed" a Houthi ballistic missile heading for the southern city of Khamis Mushait, home to a major military base.
Although Saudi Arabia has poured billions into its military, Houthi attacks continue to slip through.
"Saudi air defenses have been able to intercept some Houthi missile and drone attacks, but Saudi Arabia is so large that it's simply impossible for them to consistently defend themselves," said Thomas Juneau, security analyst at Ottawa University.
The anti-Houthi coalition called Saturday's attack a "full-fledged war crime" and vowed to "respond decisively."
Houthi media reported two Saudi strikes in Yemen's Houthi-controlled Sanaa governorate Sunday.
A spokesperson for the Houthi-run Health Ministry said on X that one of the strikes killed a civilian and wounded five others.
Saturday's attack on Riyadh drew condemnation from the United Nations and leaders around the world, including U.S. President Donald Trump, who said he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis.
Iran, which backs the Houthis, said Monday it was "deeply concerned" over the escalation.
Four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese were killed, the civil aviation authority said, with 309 people wounded.
The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia also said one of its citizens died Sunday after being wounded the day before.
Witnesses to Saturday's strike described chaos in the aftermath.
"Some had lost a hand or an arm. People were running while carrying injured people, covered in blood," a 32-year-old Riyadh resident told Agence France-Presse (AFP).
The U.S., Canadian, German and Spanish embassies in Saudi Arabia have warned their citizens to avoid Riyadh airport.
Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that has supported Yemen's government militarily since 2015, including by seeking to exert control over Yemeni airspace and the airport in the Houthi-held capital Sanaa.
Ottawa University's Juneau said the Houthis now "want to do to Saudi Arabia what Saudi Arabia does to them."
On the ground in Yemen, Saudi-supported government forces were advancing in their counteroffensive against the Houthis around the Bab el-Mandeb strait, a key shipping route, military sources said Saturday.
The Houthis claimed to have repelled them.
Claims by both sides have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult.
