high_priority_articles.title: CPI Forecasts Show Moderated Inflation in September, Keeping the Fed on Hold - Morningstar
high_priority_articles.summary: CPI Forecasts Show Moderated Inflation in September, Keeping the Fed on Hold  Morningstar
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways
- Wednesday’s CPI report is expected to show that core inflation, which excludes food and energy prices, continued to slow last month despite accelerating overall inflation, driven by surging energy prices.
- Economists are watching for signs of surging diesel prices rippling through supply chains, which would mean upward pressure on goods and services prices.
- Markets expect the Fed to leave interest rates unchanged later this month, but Bank of America economists warn a hot inflation print could revive rate hike speculation.
Economists predict Wednesday’s Consumer Price Index report will show key inflation metrics continued to moderate in September, giving Federal Reserve officials breathing room to advocate for a patient approach to future rate hikes.
Wednesday’s report comes as investors attempt to predict the Fed’s next move. Last month, the Federal Open Market Committee, citing stubbornly high inflation and a stable labor market, raised interest rates by a quarter point and penciled in at least one more hike. Officials are focused on reigning in rising prices, and this week’s CPI and Producer Price Index data will be the last inflation readings they get before their next meeting in late October.
For September, economists expect CPI to increase 0.5% after rising 0.4% in August, according to FactSet. Elevated energy prices are expected to drive the year-over-year inflation rate to 3.6% from 3.4% in August. Core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, is seen rising 0.2% in September, a slowdown from August’s 0.3%. The annual core inflation rate is expected to hold steady at 2.4%.
“You’ve seen supply shocks create a sticky situation,” says Jeffrey Schulze, head investment strategist at the Franklin Templeton Institute, referring to oil supply disruptions in the Middle East, AI-related electronics shortages, and tariff shocks. “But as we move toward 2027, some of these risks are going to start to moderate,” he says. That moderation may already be underway. “I think you see softening across the board [in September].”
September CPI Inflation Report Highlights
- CPI report date and time: Wednesday, Oct. 15, 2026, at 8:30 a.m. EDT.
- CPI is forecast to increase 0.5% in September after rising 0.4% in August.
- Core CPI is expected to rise 0.2% over the month after increasing 0.3% in August.
- CPI is predicted to rise 3.6% year over year after posting a 3.4% increase in August.
- Core CPI is forecast to increase 2.4% over the year, unchanged from August’s rate.
Core Inflation Seen Continuing to Moderate
Though high energy prices are expected to keep overall inflation elevated, economists expect prices to cool under the surface.
Policymakers have been watching core prices closely for evidence businesses are passing higher oil and diesel prices along to consumers rather than absorbing them at the expense of margins. Economists say the oil price shock’s second-order effects are most visible in airfares, which rose more than 2% in both July and August. But they haven’t seen much pass-through in other categories this year, and they don’t believe last month was any different. “I think that’s going to be something that potentially shows up closer toward the end of the year, rather than in the September release,” says Franklin Templeton’s Schulze.
Officials have been eyeing the AI data center buildout for the same reason. Surging demand for semiconductors, networking equipment, and other data center hardware has driven up prices on consumer and industrial electronics. In their September meeting, policymakers judged that AI-related price pressures were increasing and blunting some of the benefits of waning tariff-related pressures.
“Second-round inflation effects from higher energy prices and AI-related demand should remain relatively contained,” wrote Bank of America economists in a recent note. But they warned that “risks appear modestly skewed to the upside,” and could result in a second consecutive 0.3% month-over-month increase in core prices.
While oil and AI spending threaten to aggravate core inflation, many economists and officials are confident that wages are not currently a source of inflation pressure. Some officials last month described wage growth as “moderate and consistent with inflation moving toward 2%.” That assessment was supported by September’s jobs report, which showed job gains and wage growth were weaker than expected. According to Schulze, the report “suggests demand-driven inflation through the labor market is not problematic from the Fed’s vantage point.”
What the September CPI Report Could Mean for the Fed
Wednesday’s inflation data will loom large over the Fed’s deliberations when officials meet again on Oct. 27 and 28. Last month, policymakers voted unanimously to raise rates for the first time since 2023. Chair Kevin Warsh indicated that stubborn inflation was the main factor in that decision.
Policymakers signaled to markets that September’s hike likely would not be a one-off. In their quarterly Summary of Economic Projections, most officials predicted raising rates by another quarter point before the end of the year. A few signaled they were open to hiking by half a point, and two indicated they were comfortable leaving rates unchanged for the rest of 2026.
Investors immediately priced in additional increases after the Fed’s September hike, but the market’s confidence in that call was shaken by dovish remarks from several officials and September’s soft jobs report, which economists say gives the central bank room to be patient. As of Monday, investors saw a 22% chance of an October hike, down from 55% immediately following the Fed’s September rate call.
“I think that the Fed stays on hold [in October], barring an upside surprise that’s meaningfully more than consensus is expecting,” says Franklin Templeton’s Schulze.
BofA economists say a hot core inflation reading “would likely revive speculation that the Fed may need to continue its tightening cycle” this month. That speculation could nudge Treasury yields (already hovering near multidecade highs) even higher and weigh on equities.

Asia news for October 12, 2026: China-EU trade negotiations, India’s inflation and protests, North Korean missiles, and Singapore’s AI warnings
NetNewsLedger International News | Monday, October 12, 2026
THUNDER BAY, ON — Asia’s largest economies are facing a week of growing political, economic and security challenges as trade disputes, inflation, artificial intelligence and military tensions reshape the region.
For Monday, October 12, 2026, the leading developments across Singapore, China, India and Japan include a new China-European Union trade arrangement, widespread political protests in India, North Korean ballistic missile launches near Japan, and warnings from Singapore’s leaders about the impact of artificial intelligence on employment.
The news matters far beyond Asia. Decisions being made in Beijing, New Delhi, Singapore and Tokyo could influence Canadian manufacturers, Ontario’s critical minerals industry, global investment and the cost of imported goods.
For Northwestern Ontario, where mining, forestry, transportation and international trade remain essential parts of the economy, developments in Asian markets deserve close attention.
Singapore: Artificial Intelligence, Economic Growth and Public Health
1. President Tharman warns artificial intelligence is threatening entry-level jobs
Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam delivered a warning at the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok on Monday.
Speaking about the growing use of artificial intelligence, Tharman said governments need to address a decline in demand for workers entering the labour market.
New university graduates may be among the first to experience the change, as businesses turn to automated systems for tasks previously handled by junior employees.
The Singapore president also warned that AI could widen economic divisions between richer countries and developing nations.
The concern is not simply that existing jobs will disappear. It is that young workers could lose the entry-level opportunities that traditionally allow them to gain experience and advance into better-paying careers.
The issue has become an international economic challenge as companies invest heavily in AI systems that can handle research, financial analysis, customer service and administrative work.
2. Prime Minister Lawrence Wong calls for AI to strengthen society
Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong is also urging businesses and educators to use artificial intelligence without sacrificing the development of human skills.
Wong said Singapore must protect basic learning in schools and ensure employers continue training and mentoring junior employees.
His government’s approach places emphasis on retraining, fair treatment of displaced workers and regional digital cooperation through the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
The message is that Singapore wants to benefit from AI-driven growth without allowing technology to weaken education or eliminate pathways into employment.
3. Singapore faces an important monetary policy decision on October 14
The Monetary Authority of Singapore is expected to tighten monetary policy when it releases its next decision on Wednesday, October 14.
All 10 economists surveyed by Reuters before the meeting expected further tightening.
Singapore’s economy has benefited from strong investment in technology and AI infrastructure, but rising energy prices and food supply risks have created fresh inflation concerns.
Unlike the Bank of Canada, Singapore’s central bank primarily manages monetary conditions through the exchange rate rather than a conventional policy interest rate.
Economists are watching whether the authority will allow the Singapore dollar to appreciate more quickly to help control the cost of imported goods.
4. Smoke and haze raise health concerns
Singapore is also dealing with unhealthy air quality linked to regional haze.
The government has activated medical subsidy measures beginning October 12 to help eligible residents seek treatment for haze-related health problems.
The environmental problem has affected transportation, with Malaysian carrier Firefly cancelling flights between Seletar and Subang airports as a safety precaution.
The situation illustrates how air pollution crossing international borders can affect public health, business operations and transportation across Southeast Asia.

high_priority_articles.title: India-Chile trade negotiations: A quiet and strategic deal beyond tariffs - The Economic Times
high_priority_articles.summary: India-Chile trade negotiations: A quiet and strategic deal beyond tariffs  The Economic Times
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The India-Chile trade relationship is not a new one. The two countries signed a PTA in 2006, which was expanded in 2016 to cover nearly 1,800 tariff lines. That arrangement reduced tariffs on select goods and widened market access but remained limited in scope. Further, to enhance economic integration and cooperation, in May 2025, both countries signed a framework agreement for CEPA, which would include several sectors, including digital services, investment promotion and cooperation, MSMEs, critical minerals, etc.
Though trade between the two nations has grown steadily, it has remained relatively small compared to other trading partners. Exports to Chile account for just 0.2-0.3% of India’s export basket, while Chile exports around 2-3% of its total exports to India by value. Chile’s exports are very concentrated, with China occupying around 40% of its exports. Chile’s export basket to India is dominated by copper and related minerals, alongside chemicals and some agricultural products. India, in turn, exports pharmaceuticals, automobiles, particularly two- and three-wheelers, textiles, and engineering goods. Though this relationship may not be trade-heavy, it is trade-compatible. And in the era of energy transition, that compatibility requires a dimension: improved market access with supply-chain resilience.
Chile holds some of the world’s largest lithium reserves and is a major global producer of copper. These are not ordinary commodities; they are critical inputs for industry and the global net-carbon neutrality goals. Lithium is central to electric vehicle (EV) batteries, grid storage systems, and renewable energy apparatus. Copper is also indispensable for power transmission, EV charging infrastructure, and the expansion of electricity grids. In a rapidly changing world, metal and mineral security has become synonymous with industrial security.
In this respect, India’s ambitions are clear. It aims to scale up EV adoption, expand solar and wind capacity, build domestic battery manufacturing under production-linked incentive (PLI) schemes, and reduce import dependence in critical sectors. However, secure, sustainable, and diversified access to critical minerals and metals, such as lithium and copper, is essential for realising these ambitions. At present, global mining, processing, and refining capacities for many critical minerals are highly concentrated, creating vulnerabilities in supply chains. For India, expanding partnerships with resource-rich countries like Chile is not only about lowering tariffs; it is also about building long-term supply chain resilience amid a fragmenting world order.
Additionally, there is a larger geopolitical context. Much of the recent global discourse on critical minerals has been framed through strategic competition among major powers, like China and the US. India-Chile cooperation offers a different model, which is rooted in Global South collaboration rather than bloc politics. It demonstrates that strategic supply chains can be diversified through pragmatic economic partnerships, without being a part of geopolitical blocs.
Ultimately, the success of the India-Chile agreement will depend on how negotiators treat it. Though lowering or eliminating the tariff and non-tariff barriers for the merchandise trade may bring welfare effects for both countries, a strategic expansion rather than a conventional one would anchor a long-term industrial partnership.
If designed with foresight, integrating trade, minerals, investment, technology, and sustainability, it could present a model for sustainable economic partnership for the Global South also. The scope of the agreement, therefore, should not remain partial. It should become strategic.
Dr. Badri Narayanan Gopalakrishnan, PhD is the Founder of Infinite Sum Modelling. Himanshu Jaiswal is Research Fellow, Infisum Modeling.

high_priority_articles.title: South Africa’s Malben, Egypt’s Elaraby eye automotive components manufacturing partnership - Engineering News
high_priority_articles.summary: South Africa’s Malben, Egypt’s Elaraby eye automotive components manufacturing partnership  Engineering News
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Malben Engineering’s Luca Smargiasso and the Elaraby Group’s Mohamed A El Araby signed a MoU in Alamein on October 2, at a ceremony witnessed by dignitaries including South Africa’s Trade, Industry and Competition Minister Parks Tau and Egypt’s Investment and Foreign Trade Minister Dr Mohamed Farid Saleh.
South African automotive components manufacturer Malben Engineering has signed an agreement with Egypt’s Elaraby Group, opening the way for the possible creation of a new venture to manufacture automotive components in the North African country.
The memorandum of understanding was initialled on the sidelines of the Africa Automotive Investment Forum, which took place in Alamein in early October and was attended by key African policymakers, original-equipment manufacturers (OEMs), investors, financiers and industrialists.
The agreement, which follows initial meetings facilitated by the African Association of Automotive Manufacturers, proposes to combine Malben Engineering’s established automotive manufacturing expertise with Elaraby Group’s extensive domestic industrial capability.
Established in Nigel in 1974, Malben Engineering has more than five decades of experience in supplying stampings and complex welded assemblies to leading OEMs operating in South Africa, including Ford Motor Company, BMW, Fiat, Alfa Romeo and Volkswagen.
The highly diversified Elaraby Group, meanwhile, operates through 16 companies spanning commercial, industrial, medical and service activities and employs more than 36 000 people in Egypt and the Middle East.
“Partnering with an established Egyptian industrial group could materially shorten Malben’s route to market and provide access to existing manufacturing capacity, people, administrative systems, procurement capability and local supplier relationships, avoiding many of the challenges associated with a greenfield startup,” Malben Engineering operational director Luca Smargiasso explains.
The Elaraby Group will contribute its established Egyptian industrial footprint, local operating capability, market knowledge and relationships.
The fact that both companies are family-owned businesses has also been cited as a factor in facilitating the relationship, with the Elaraby Group involving third-generation family members and Malben Engineering remaining a second-generation family enterprise, 52 years after its founding.
“As the partnership develops, the parties intend to explore joint investment opportunities in new facilities and capabilities serving Egypt's automotive industry, with the potential to support wider regional supply opportunities,” Smargiasso explains.
Technical director Marco Smargiasso adds that the proposed partnership is also aligned with Egypt’s National Automotive Industry Development Programme, which is designed to localise and deepen automotive manufacturing and develop the supporting components industry.
The framework links incentives to measurable outcomes, including local content, production volumes, investment and exports, and has some parallels with South Africa’s Automotive Production Development Programme.
There is also a longer-term opportunity to develop competitive African automotive supply chains through which components and manufacturing capability can increasingly be sourced within the continent rather than imported from outside Africa.
“As that capability develops, the African Continental Free Trade Agreement creates the potential to serve OEMs and automotive markets across the continent, subject to the applicable rules of origin and market-access requirements,” Smargiasso adds.
However, commercial director Marius Schafer says the immediate priority is to establish a competitive and sustainable operation in Egypt.

high_priority_articles.title: South Korea's Honam Semiconductor Power Grid: Samsung, SK Hynix to Bear 80% of 1.4 Trillion Won Cost - BigGo Finance
high_priority_articles.summary: South Korea's Honam Semiconductor Power Grid: Samsung, SK Hynix to Bear 80% of 1.4 Trillion Won Cost  BigGo Finance
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Korea Electric Power Corporation (KEPCO) confirmed that Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix will bear 80% of the 1.4 trillion won (approximately $1.1 billion) power grid construction cost required for South Korea's Honam semiconductor industrial complex. KEPCO CEO Kim Dong-chul confirmed the cost-sharing structure during a National Assembly audit by the Trade, Industry, Energy, SMEs, and Startups Committee on the 12th, explaining that it is premised on the assumption that government support under the Semiconductor Special Act will not be provided.
Responding to a question from People Power Party lawmaker Kim Do-eup about transmission facility budgets, Kim said, "KEPCO's share is less than 20%," adding that "Samsung and SK Hynix are set to bear the remainder." When lawmaker Cho Ji-yeon asked again whether it was correct that the private sector would shoulder 80% of the 1.4 trillion won, Kim confirmed, "That is correct."
He noted that the power grid in question is a dedicated line for Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, saying "the consumers are required to bear the cost." However, the Semiconductor Special Act stipulates that the national and local governments may cover 50–100% of total project costs for industrial infrastructure construction and operation needed for clusters. Kim elaborated, "If the government provides support, that is how it would work. If there is no support under the Semiconductor Special Act, KEPCO, Samsung, and SK Hynix will share the burden according to their electricity usage ratios."
During the audit, lawmaker Cho pointed out, "The president himself said the government would take responsibility for power and water," adding, "Even though the special act requires the government to bear more than 50%, KEPCO says it will cover only 20% and the companies will pay the rest." She criticized, "Ultimately, this is telling companies to invest and build all the power infrastructure themselves. They've twisted not just the companies' right arm but their left arm as well."
Prepayment Proposal Unrelated to Honam Semiconductor
Kim also made clear that the electricity bill prepayment proposal was not directly related to the Honam semiconductor complex construction. When lawmaker Yoon Han-hong asked whether KEPCO had demanded prepayment from Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix for the Honam semiconductor construction, Kim emphasized the timing showed no connection, saying, "KEPCO proposed the prepayment to the companies in March–April, while the decision to build the Honam semiconductor complex was made at the end of June."
Earlier this year, KEPCO proposed that Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix prepay 25 trillion won (approximately $18.8 billion) in electricity bills for the period from 2027 to 2031, to be paid in advance over one year. This amounts to roughly five years' worth of electricity bills for each company based on what they paid last year. When lawmaker Yoon suggested the two companies likely rejected the prepayment due to semiconductor industry uncertainty and the burden of massive capital outflows, Kim replied, "That is correct."
The KEPCO bond issuance limit was identified as the backdrop for the prepayment proposal. Kim Jae-gun, KEPCO's vice president of power systems, explained, "Our current bond ratio is 5x, and we need to reduce it to 2x by the end of 2027. We proposed this to resolve the issue on our own." CEO Kim also said, "From KEPCO's perspective, maintaining the bond issuance multiple within 2x is indeed the biggest challenge."
KEPCO's bond issuance limit is, in principle, twice the sum of its capital and reserves. However, due to the funding crunch from massive losses in 2022, the KEPCO Act was amended to temporarily allow issuance up to 5x until the end of 2027. Kim indicated that an electricity rate hike will be unavoidable once this special allowance expires.
When Democratic Party lawmaker Chung Jin-wook asked about plans to secure funding for power grid investment, Kim responded, "If the bond issuance multiple is reduced from 5x to 2x at the end of 2027, KEPCO will no longer be able to issue bonds. While self-help efforts are necessary, I believe a minimum electricity rate increase will be needed." When lawmaker Chung mentioned the need for government fiscal input, Kim nodded in agreement.
Currently, household electricity rates have been frozen for 14 consecutive quarters, and industrial rates for 8 consecutive quarters. While rate adjustments have been delayed, KEPCO's total debt has surpassed 200 trillion won (approximately $150.1 billion), with daily interest costs reaching the 10 billion won (approximately $7.5 million) range.
Power Grid Investment Remains Top Priority
Despite the financial burden, Kim stated that power grid investment will remain the top priority. "Although financial conditions are difficult in many ways, we are placing power grid investment at the highest priority," he said.
Regarding the need for redundancy in power grids supplying the Honam semiconductor industrial complex and other areas, Kim explained that the grids currently managed by KEPCO are already configured bidirectionally, so if a failure occurs on one side, the other grid can temporarily compensate. "There are almost no single-line grids currently managed by KEPCO," Kim added.
Meanwhile, regarding the government's Public Official Ethics Committee decision to deny employment approval for former South Jeolla Province Governor Kim Young-rok, who had been mentioned as a potential successor, Kim briefly stated, "I understand there were issues in the subsequent personnel process."
The Honam semiconductor industrial complex is a region where Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix have announced large-scale investments, and infrastructure expansion including power and water has been identified as a key variable determining the project's success. SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won visited the Honam semiconductor site on the 9th and repeatedly raised power and water supply issues.
The cost-sharing structure revealed during this National Assembly audit could change depending on whether support under the Semiconductor Special Act is provided. If the national and local governments cover 50–100% of total project costs under the special act, the burden on companies and KEPCO would be significantly reduced. Conversely, if special act support is not provided, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix would have to bear more than 1.1 trillion won (approximately $825.7 million) of the 1.4 trillion won total.

EU officials spoke of a ‘paradigm shift’ in wake of surprise trade deal, saying the ‘nature of the rebalancing exercise has changed’
Weeks of high-wire negotiations between China and the EU culminated in a surprise trade deal that will, among other measures, impose strict quotas on Chinese hybrid car exports to the bloc and slash Chinese tariffs on a variety of European goods.
The deal, unveiled on Friday, takes some of the heat out of searing bilateral trade tensions and temporarily averts the prospect of a bruising trade war.
Beijing agreed not to retaliate against Brussels’ move to curb imports of Chinese hybrid cars, which will see shipments capped at 350,000 units per year, rising at 6 per cent annually. This will leave exports at less than half the 800,000 vehicles the EU has projected will be shipped in 2026.
Asked on Monday how Beijing grew to accept the concessions – after Chinese officials spent weeks rejecting the prospect of voluntarily limiting auto shipments – Brussels framed its position with a time-worn business maxim: “The customer is always right.”

Some parents have suggested closing schools for several consecutive days to make it easier for families to make arrangements, said Malaysia Education Minister Fadhlina Sidek.
SINGAPORE: Malaysia's education minister on Monday (Oct 12) defended its day-to-day approach to school closures, as parents called for more certainty over arrangements during the worsening haze.
In a Facebook post, Education Minister Fadhlina Sidek said some parents had suggested closing schools for several consecutive days to make it easier for families to plan ahead.
But decisions have to take into account fluctuating air quality and the disruption that prolonged closures could cause to students’ learning, she said.
“In making decisions, it is important to understand the air pollutant index (API) readings can change depending on time and location,” she said.
School closures must therefore take into account the prevailing conditions in each area, she added.
“I understand these concerns. That’s why I have requested that decisions on school closures be announced as early as possible to give parents time to prepare,” said Fadhlina.
Haze management also involves several agencies, she explained, with the environment department responsible for monitoring air quality and addressing pollution while the health ministry provides the public with guidance on health risks.
The education ministry, meanwhile, focuses on students’ safety and the management of school operations based on prevailing conditions, she said.
Fadhlina also pointed to the impact of prolonged school disruptions during the COVID-19 pandemic.
“Until today, efforts to address learning loss (during COVID-19) are still ongoing. Lost learning time is not easily recovered, especially since access to home-based teaching and learning facilities is not the same for all students,” she said.
For boarding school students, the ministry’s recommendation is that they remain in their hostels during haze-related school closures as long as the conditions are safe.
“The education ministry does not want parents to be burdened with repeatedly picking up and sending their children back to school,” Fadhlina said.
Malaysia has 68 air quality monitoring stations nationwide under its Environmental Quality Monitoring Programme.
Under the education ministry’s guidelines, schools in areas with API readings above 180 must close. Schools will also close if readings remain above 150 for three consecutive days.
The worsening haze has prompted school closures in several states across Peninsular Malaysia since last week, with announcements made a day before.
Schools in Melaka, Negeri Sembilan, Pahang, Putrajaya alongside parts of Kuala Lumpur and Selangor resumed in-person classes on Monday after API readings on Sunday improved to moderate levels, local media reported.
In Johor, however, which remains the worst-affected state, all schools and educational institutions will remain closed for another five days from Oct 12 to Oct 16.
Johor began closing schools on Thursday. Several other affected states and areas followed suit on Friday.
The education ministry has said that state authorities will decide on school closures based on haze conditions, according to local media.
